title: The Serpent, the Fruit, and the Way Out of Eden
summary: A crafty serpent questions God's word, and the woman and the man eat from the forbidden tree. Their eyes are opened, they hide from God, and when he confronts them each shifts the blame. God pronounces judgment on the serpent, the woman, and the man, promises that the woman's seed will crush the serpent's head, clothes the couple with garments of skin, and sends them out of the garden, with cherubim guarding the way to the tree of life.
story: Chapter 2 ended with a man and a woman naked and unashamed in a garden full of good gifts, under one command. Chapter 3 tells how that world was lost. It is the hinge between creation and everything after it. From here on, the Bible's story is about a good world gone wrong and a God who will not let it go. Death, pain, hard labor, broken relationships, and distance from God all enter here, and they will spread fast in the chapters that follow. But so does grace: God comes looking, he speaks a promise about the serpent's defeat, and he makes clothes for the people he is sending away.
historical:
The chapter belongs to the same early material as chapter 2, and like it, it speaks to a world full of stories about serpents, trees, and lost chances at life. In the Epic of Gilgamesh, the hero finally obtains a plant that restores youth, only to have a snake steal it while he bathes, so that humans lose the chance to escape death. In Egypt the cobra rose from the crown of Pharaoh as a symbol of royal power, and the great serpent Apophis was the enemy of the sun god. Serpents could stand for wisdom, healing, fertility, or chaos, depending on the story. Genesis is careful about what it does with this image. The serpent is a creature, one of the beasts of the field that the LORD God had made, not a rival god, and it has no power except the power of suggestion.

Genesis itself does not name the serpent as Satan. Later Jewish writers began to connect the two, and the New Testament makes the link openly when Revelation calls the devil “that ancient serpent” (Revelation 12:9; 20:2). The cherubim of verse 24 also belong to the ancient world. Assyrian palaces were guarded by huge winged figures with human heads and animal bodies, and Israel's own tabernacle and temple had cherubim over the ark and woven into the curtain that barred the way into the Most Holy Place.
cultural:
An ancient reader would have understood nakedness and clothing as matters of status and honor, not only of modesty. To be stripped was to be shamed, and to clothe someone was an act of care or of investiture, as when a king clothed a servant he honored. So it matters that the couple's first act after eating is to cover themselves with fig leaves, which are large enough to be sewn into rough coverings, and that God's last act before sending them out is to make them better garments from skin. The phrase in the breeze of the day is usually taken to mean the cool part of the afternoon or evening; a minority of scholars read it as the wind of a storm, a sign of God coming in judgment.

The judgments speak to the core of each person's life in an agricultural world. For the woman, the pain touches bearing children and her closest relationship. For the man, the ground itself now resists him, producing thorns and thistles, and bread comes only through sweat. The same Hebrew word for painful toil (itsavon) is used for her childbearing and his farming. Both have become harder, and death, the return to dust, waits at the end.
literary: The chapter is a finely built drama. The serpent's first line is a question that twists God's word: God had given every tree but one, and the serpent asks whether he forbade them all. The woman corrects it but adds a detail of her own (or touch it) and softens the penalty. Verse 6 echoes 2:9 almost word for word, now seen through desire: good for food, pleasing to the eyes, desirable for wisdom. The promise that their eyes will be opened comes true with bitter irony, since what they see is their own nakedness. Then the order of the story reverses. The sin moved from serpent to woman to man; God's questions move from man to woman to serpent; and the judgments move back again, from serpent to woman to man, a mirrored pattern (a chiasm) that puts the questioning at the center. Verse 15 and the judgments of verses 14 to 19 are set as poetry, and the chapter ends with a guarded road east, the direction of exile in Genesis.

outline.t: They eat, and their eyes are opened
God seeks them, and they shift the blame
The serpent cursed and the promise of the woman's seed
Pain in childbirth, toil on the ground, return to dust
Eve named, the couple clothed and sent from the garden

doctrines.note: Sin begins not with a crime but with a question about whether God can be trusted, followed by the choice to decide good and evil for oneself. Its results are immediate: shame, fear, hiding, blame, and broken relationships with God, with one another, and with the ground. The church has read this chapter as the origin of the human condition, though traditions differ on how Adam's sin is passed on.

God said that in the day they ate they would surely die, and they did not drop dead that day. Readers have answered this in several ways: that the phrase can mean simply when you eat, that death as mortality and separation from God began that day, and that God's mercy delayed the full sentence. The judgments are real, but the man and woman are not themselves cursed; the curse falls on the serpent and the ground.

Verse 15 promises lasting conflict between the serpent's seed and the woman's, ending with the serpent's head crushed. It is the first hint in Scripture that God will defeat evil through a human descendant, and Christians have long read it as the first announcement of the gospel.

Before the couple leaves the garden, God has already begun to act for them. He seeks them out with a question, promises a victory over the serpent, and covers their shame with garments he makes himself. Grace appears in the same chapter as the fall.

words.note: Arum, translated crafty. The word can be positive (prudent, shrewd, as often in Proverbs) or negative. It is a deliberate echo of arummim, naked, in 2:25. The couple were naked and unashamed; the serpent was shrewd. By the end of the scene they have gained a kind of knowing and lost their innocence.

Zera, seed or offspring. Like the English word, it can mean one descendant or a whole line of them. In verse 15 it begins a thread that runs through Genesis, as God promises seed to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Whether the woman's seed means humanity in general, the line of the faithful, or one particular descendant is debated, and the grammar allows the singular he who crushes the serpent's head.

Teshuqah, desire, used only three times in the Hebrew Bible (here, 4:7, and Song of Songs 7:10). Some read it in verse 16 as the woman's longing for her husband, which he will exploit by ruling over her. Others, noting that in 4:7 sin's desire is to master Cain, read it as a desire to control that meets domination in return. On both readings the verse describes a relationship bent by sin, not God's original design.

Arar, to curse, to place under a ban or bind with misfortune. It is the opposite of the blessing God spoke in chapter 1. Here it falls on the serpent and on the ground because of the man, and it will fall on Cain in 4:11. The call of Abraham in chapter 12 will answer this spreading curse with a fivefold promise of blessing.

christ: Christian readers since at least the second century have called verse 15 the first gospel. The New Testament does not quote the verse directly, but it echoes it: Paul tells the Roman church, “The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet” (Romans 16:20), and Hebrews says Christ shared our humanity “so that by His death He might destroy him who holds the power of death, that is, the devil” (Hebrews 2:14). Paul's fullest reading of this chapter comes in Romans 5, where he sets Adam and Christ side by side: “For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one man the many will be made righteous” (Romans 5:19). He says the same in brief: “For as in Adam all die, so in Christ all will be made alive” (1 Corinthians 15:22). Many readers have also noticed that the first Adam failed in a garden of plenty while Christ stood firm when tempted in the wilderness, a thematic contrast rather than a prediction. The Bible's final vision answers the end of this chapter, with the tree of life open again and the words “No longer will there be any curse” (Revelation 22:3).

hard.q: Were Adam and Eve real people, and does it matter?
hard.a:
Christians who share the same confession about sin and salvation answer this in more than one way. The traditional view, held by most of the church through its history, takes Adam and Eve as the first human pair and the actual parents of the whole race, whose sin affected all their descendants. A second view, held by some who accept an ancient human population on scientific grounds, sees Adam and Eve as a real couple whom God chose from among early humans to represent humanity, so that their fall was a real event in history with effects on all. A third view reads the chapter as a story about every human being (Adam simply means human), shaped in ancient Near Eastern style to show what sin is and what it does, without requiring two individual ancestors.

Those who insist on a historical Adam point to Paul, who builds his argument in Romans 5 and 1 Corinthians 15 on one man's disobedience and one man's obedience, and to Luke's genealogy, which traces Jesus back to Adam. Those who read the chapter differently argue that Paul could use Adam as Scripture presents him without settling modern questions of human origins. What all these readers affirm is what the chapter plainly teaches: humanity was made good, turned from God by its own choice, and cannot undo the damage by itself.

questions: The serpent's first move is a question about what God really said and whether he can be trusted. Where do you hear that question most loudly in your own life?
The man blames the woman, and the woman blames the serpent. Why is shifting blame such an instinctive response, and what would it look like to answer God honestly?
Before sending the couple out, God makes them clothing. What does that act suggest about how God treats people even when he judges them?
